paragraphs: When the revolution that overturns the social and political state of an aristocratic people begins to reach literature, it usually shows itself first in the drama, and it always remains most visible there. A spectator at a play is, to some extent, taken by surprise by the impression it makes on him. He has no time to consult his memory or to ask people better qualified to judge than he is. It does not occur to him to resist the new literary tendencies he begins to feel; he gives in to them before he knows what they are. Authors are very quick to discover which way the public’s taste is secretly turning. They shape their works accordingly, and the literature of the stage, after serving as a sign of the coming literary revolution, soon carries it through. If you want to judge in advance the literature of a people that is sliding into democracy, study its plays.

Moreover, even among aristocratic nations, the literature of the stage is the most democratic part of their literature. No kind of literary pleasure is so easily within the reach of the multitude as the pleasure of watching a theatrical performance. It requires neither preparation nor study to enjoy; it takes hold of you in the midst of your prejudices and your ignorance. When an as yet untutored love of the pleasures of the mind begins to stir in one class of the community, it draws that class straight to the stage. The theaters of aristocratic nations have always been full of spectators who did not belong to the aristocracy. The theater is the only place where the higher ranks mix with the middle and lower classes, and the only place where the higher ranks agree to listen to the opinions of the others, or at least allow them to have an opinion at all. In the theater, cultivated men with literary accomplishments have always had more trouble than anywhere else in making their taste prevail over that of the people, and in avoiding being swept along by it. The pit has often made laws for the boxes.

If it is hard for an aristocracy to keep the people from getting the upper hand in the theater, it is easy to see that the people will be supreme there once democratic principles have worked their way into the laws and customs. That happens when ranks are mixed together, when minds as well as fortunes are drawn closer, and when the upper class has lost its hereditary wealth along with its power, its precedents, and its leisure. The tastes and inclinations that come naturally to democratic nations in literature will therefore show themselves first in the drama, and we can foresee that they will burst out there with great force. In written works, the literary rules of aristocracy will be modified gently, gradually, and, so to speak, legally; in the theater they will be overthrown in a riot. The drama brings out most of the good qualities and almost all the faults that are inherent in democratic literature. Democratic peoples place a very low value on learning and care little about what happened in Rome and Athens. They want to hear something that concerns themselves, and what they demand is a portrayal of the present age.

When the heroes and manners of antiquity are often brought onto the stage, and playwrights faithfully follow the rules of old precedent, that is enough to conclude that the democratic classes have not yet gained the upper hand in the theaters. In the preface to “Britannicus,” Racine very humbly apologizes for having placed Junia among the Vestals, who, according to Aulus Gellius, he says, “admitted no one below six years of age nor above ten.” We may be sure he would neither have accused himself of this offense nor defended himself against criticism if he had been writing for our contemporaries. A fact of this kind shows the state of literature at the time, and it shows the state of society itself as well. A democratic stage does not prove that the nation is in a democratic state, because, as we have just seen, even in aristocracies democratic tastes may influence the drama. But when the spirit of aristocracy reigns exclusively on the stage, that fact proves beyond refutation that the whole of society is aristocratic. One may boldly infer that the same lettered and learned class that sways the playwrights also commands the people and governs the country.

The refined tastes and arrogant bearing of an aristocracy will rarely fail to lead it, when it controls the stage, to make a kind of selection within human nature. Some conditions of society hold its chief interest, and the scenes that depict their manners are preferred on the stage. Certain virtues, and even certain vices, are thought to deserve a place there more than others, and these are applauded while all the rest are shut out. On the stage as elsewhere, an aristocratic audience wants to meet only people of quality and to share the emotions of kings. The same goes for style: an aristocracy tends to impose on playwrights certain modes of expression that set the key in which everything must be delivered. In this way the stage often comes to depict only one side of man, or sometimes even to represent what cannot be found in human nature at all, rising above nature and going beyond it.

In democratic communities the spectators have no such favorites, and they rarely show such dislikes. They like to see on the stage the medley of conditions, feelings, and opinions that they see before their own eyes. The drama becomes more striking, more ordinary, and more true. Sometimes, however, those who write for the stage in democracies also go beyond the limits of human nature, but on a different side from their predecessors. In trying to represent in minute detail the small oddities of the moment and the particular traits of certain characters, they forget to portray the general features of the race.

When the democratic classes rule the stage, they bring as much license into the way subjects are treated as into the choice of them. The love of the drama is, of all literary tastes, the one most natural to democratic nations, so in these communities the number of authors, of spectators, and of theatrical performances keeps growing. A multitude made up of such different elements, and scattered over so many different places, cannot recognize the same rules or submit to the same laws. No agreement is possible among so many judges, who do not know when they will meet again, and so each one pronounces his own sentence on the play. The general effect of democracy is to call into question the authority of all literary rules and conventions. On the stage it abolishes them altogether and puts nothing in their place but the whim of each author and each public.

The drama also shows in a particular way the truth of what I said earlier, when I spoke more generally about style and art in democratic literature. Read the criticisms provoked by the plays of the age of Louis XIV, and you are surprised to notice how much stress the public put on the probability of the plot. You notice the importance attached to the perfect consistency of the characters, and to their doing nothing that could not be easily explained and understood. The value placed on forms of language at that time, and the petty quarrels over words with which playwrights were attacked, are no less surprising. It seems that the men of the age of Louis XIV attached exaggerated importance to details that can be noticed in the study but escape attention on the stage. For, after all, the main purpose of a play is to be performed, and its chief merit is to move the audience. But in that age the audience and the readers were the same people: on leaving the theater, they summoned the author to judgment at their own firesides. In democracies, plays are listened to but not read. Most of those who go to the theater do not go to look for the pleasures of the mind but for the keen emotions of the heart. They do not expect to hear a fine piece of literature but to see a play. As long as the author writes his country’s language correctly enough to be understood, and his characters arouse curiosity and awaken sympathy, the audience is satisfied. They ask nothing more of fiction and go straight back to real life. Correctness of style is therefore less required, because careful observance of its rules is less noticeable on the stage. As for the probability of the plot, it is incompatible with constant novelty, surprise, and quickness of invention. It is therefore neglected, and the public excuses the neglect. You may be sure that if you bring your audience face to face with something that moves them, they will not care by what road you brought them there, and they will never reproach you for stirring their emotions in spite of the rules of drama.

The Americans show very clearly all the different inclinations I have just described when they go to the theater. But it must be admitted that so far very few of them go to the theater at all. Playgoers and plays have increased enormously in the United States over the last forty years, yet the population indulges in this kind of amusement with the greatest reserve. This is due to particular causes that the reader already knows, and a few words will be enough to remind him of them. The Puritans who founded the American republics were not only enemies of amusements; they professed a special horror of the stage. They regarded it as an abominable pastime, and as long as their principles held undivided sway, theatrical performances were completely unknown among them. These opinions of the first fathers of the colony have left very deep marks on the minds of their descendants. The extreme regularity of habits and great strictness of manners seen in the United States have so far put further obstacles in the way of the growth of dramatic art. There are no dramatic subjects in a country that has seen no great political catastrophes and where love always leads by a straight and easy road to marriage. People who spend every weekday making money and Sunday going to church have nothing to attract the muse of Comedy.

One fact is enough to show that the stage is not very popular in the United States. The Americans, whose laws allow the utmost freedom and even license of language in every other respect, have nevertheless subjected their playwrights to a kind of censorship. Theatrical performances can only take place with the permission of the municipal authorities. This may show how much communities resemble individuals. They surrender without scruple to their ruling passions, and then take the greatest care not to yield too much to the force of tastes they do not have.

No part of literature is joined by closer or more numerous ties to the present condition of society than the drama. The drama of one period can never suit the following age if, in the meantime, an important revolution has changed the nation’s manners and laws. The great authors of an earlier age may still be read, but plays written for a different public will not be followed. The playwrights of the past live only in books. The traditional taste of certain individuals, vanity, fashion, or the genius of an actor may sustain or revive the aristocratic drama for a time in a democracy. But it will soon fall away of its own accord, not overthrown but abandoned.
